artiest/benga.text:
Benga, real name Adegbenga Otomayomi Adejumo, is a British musician from Croydon, born in 1986 and a pioneer of dubstep production. He has Yoruba ancestors from Nigeria. Inspired by the UK garage producer Wookie, as a teenager he made music on a PlayStation and later with FruityLoops. In the record shop Big Apple in Croydon he met Skream, and together they helped shape the sound of dubstep that emerged in the early 2000s. DJ Hatcha, who worked in the shop, heard his productions, and by the age of fifteen Benga had made his first record.

His second record was The Judgement, with Skream. Releases on Big Apple Records, Hotflush Recordings and Planet Mu followed. In 2006 he released his debut album Newstep himself. With Coki of Digital Mystikz he made Night, which in 2008 reached number 98 in the British chart. In 2007 he formed the dubstep supergroup Magnetic Man with Skream and Artwork, which released an EP in 2009 and an album in 2010. He also produced Katy on a Mission by Katy B, which reached number five in 2010. From 2011 he presented a show on BBC Radio 1 with Skream. His third album Chapter II came out in 2013 on Sony Music, with the single Forefather featuring Kano.

Benga is one of the producers who turned dubstep from an underground style in South London into a worldwide genre. In 2012 he said he no longer wanted to call his music dubstep, in order to stay creative. His work shows how a teenager with a games console could help build a new club style.
artiest/benga.listen: Listen to Night by Benga and Coki from 2008. Notice the deep, slow bass and the space between the beats, typical of early dubstep.

artiest/benga-en-coki.text:
Benga and Coki are two producers from early London dubstep. Benga, whose real name is Adegbenga Adejumo, was born in 1986 in Croydon, in south London, and has Nigerian Yoruba roots. As a teenager he began making beats, first on a PlayStation and then with FruityLoops. In the record shop Big Apple in Croydon he met Skream, and together they helped shape the sound of dubstep that emerged in the early 2000s. At fifteen he made his first record, Skank, released in 2002. Coki came from the duo Digital Mystikz.

Their joint track Night from 2007 is their best-known work. It reached number 98 in the British chart in 2008, remarkable for a style that then still came from the underground. Benga later released albums such as Newstep (2006) and Diary of an Afro Warrior (2008), and together with Skream and Artwork formed the group Magnetic Man. He also produced Katy on a Mission, Katy B's debut.

Dubstep is based on slow, heavy bass lines, ample space between the beats and a rhythm that feels half as fast as the beat itself. Night shows how the style broke out of the London clubs to a larger audience, and Benga and Coki are among the makers who made that possible.
artiest/benga-en-coki.listen: Listen to Night. Notice the low, rolling bass and the silence between the beats, which gives the track space and tension.

artiest/benjamin-britten.text:
Benjamin Britten was an English composer, conductor and pianist and a central figure in British music of the twentieth century. He was born in 1913 in the fishing town of Lowestoft in Suffolk, on the feast day of St Cecilia, the patron saint of music. He studied at the Royal College of Music in London and privately with Frank Bridge. He first attracted attention in 1934 with the a cappella work A Boy Was Born. With the premiere of the opera Peter Grimes in 1945 he became internationally famous.

In the thirty years that followed he wrote a further fourteen operas, in addition to orchestral, choral, solo vocal and chamber music and film music. Well-known works are the War Requiem of 1962 and The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra, an orchestral piece that introduces the instruments one by one. He liked writing for children and amateurs, for example the opera Noye's Fludde, the Missa Brevis and the song collection Friday Afternoons, and he often composed with particular performers in mind. His most important muse was his life and working partner, the tenor Peter Pears. Together with Pears and Eric Crozier he founded the Aldeburgh Festival in 1948, and in 1967 he had the concert hall Snape Maltings built. In 1976 he became the first composer to be given a peerage for life, a life peerage, shortly before his death at the age of sixty-three.

Britten brought opera and choral singing in England back to a high level and showed that serious music can also be written for children and amateurs. As a result his work can still be heard today in the concert hall and in education.
artiest/benjamin-britten.listen: Listen to The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra. Notice how each instrument group and each instrument in turn plays the theme, and how the fugue at the end brings everything together again.

artiest/benjamin-herman.text: The alto saxophonist Benjamin Herman was born in London and grew up in Amsterdam. He founded the New Cool Collective, a group that mixes jazz with Latin, soul and dance music in the spirit of acid jazz. He also makes albums under his own name, such as Campert, with words by the poet Remco Campert, and Bughouse (2018), with the guitarist Reinier Baas. Herman is a fixture on Dutch stages and at festivals, and plays both hard bop and funky dance music.
artiest/benjamin-herman.listen: Listen to the swinging alto sax over a danceable Latin groove.

artiest/bennie-jolink.text:
Bennie Jolink was born in 1946 in Hummelo, in the Achterhoek. He attended the art academy in Enschede and taught drawing and painting. He then played in the band Puddingh. When it broke up in 1974, he founded Normaal with the drummer Jan Manschot and a few band members. Jolink became the singer and guitarist, and from the start the great driving force.

Normaal first sang in English. But when in 1975 at a pop festival in Lochem Jolink launched into a blues in the Achterhoek dialect, it went down so well that the band kept singing in its own dialect from then on. It was a reaction to disco and glam rock, and to the way the west of the country looked down on people from the eastern regions. The breakthrough came in 1977 with Oerend hard, about two motorcyclists who had never heard of riding slowly. The music was solid rock with influences of country and boogie, and the concerts in big party tents in the countryside became notorious. Jolink even invented a word of his own for it, høken, which found its way into the dictionary.

Normaal became one of the Dutch bands with the most Top 40 hits, although the group never reached number one. In 2015 the band gave a farewell concert in the GelreDome, and in 2016 Jolink stopped performing for health reasons. He received an Edison for his entire body of work in 2006. Jolink gave the regional language a place in Nederpop and is regarded as the founder of boerenrock, or 'farmers' rock'.
artiest/bennie-jolink.listen: Listen to Oerend hard by Normaal. Notice the driving guitars and the racing rhythm, which evoke the feeling of a fast motorbike, and the Achterhoek lyrics that Jolink sings with great bravura.

artiest/bennie-maupin.text: Bennie Maupin from Detroit plays saxophones, flute and above all bass clarinet. His dark, shifting bass clarinet can be heard on Miles Davis's Bitches Brew (1970). He then played in Herbie Hancock's sextet and in his band the Headhunters, with whom he recorded Head Hunters in 1973. In 1974 he recorded The Jewel in the Lotus for ECM, a calm and spacious album that is almost the opposite of Hancock's funk. Maupin often works with small motifs and tonal colours rather than long solos.
artiest/bennie-maupin.listen: Listen to the bass clarinet moving low and soft through the sound.

artiest/bennie-moten.text:
Benjamin Moten was born in 1893 in Kansas City, Missouri, and grew up in the same city. As a pianist and bandleader he built up the Kansas City Orchestra, the leading regional blues orchestra of the Midwest in the 1920s. He made his first recordings on 23 September 1923 for OKeh. They still sounded like the New Orleans jazz of King Oliver and others, with the influence of ragtime and the stomping beat for which the band was known. In 1926 the orchestra signed with Victor.

In 1929 Count Basie, the bassist Walter Page and the trumpeter Oran Hot Lips Page joined. Page's walking bass gave the music a completely new feel, unlike the tuba that had previously played the rhythm, and Basie's sparing, syncopated piano runs coloured the whole. The singer Jimmy Rushing also joined. At the last session on 13 December 1932, in Camden, New Jersey, Moten did not play himself. The arrangements were largely by Eddie Durham, and the recordings included numbers that became swing classics, among them Moten Swing.

Moten died in 1935 after a failed tonsillectomy. His orchestra helped to develop the riff style that later defined many big bands of the 1930s. In those last sessions something of what later became the Basie sound could already be heard, four years before Basie recorded under his own name.
artiest/bennie-moten.listen: Listen to Moten Swing from 1932. Notice the walking bass that carries the number and the short, repeated riffs of the horns answering one another.

artiest/bennie-moten-s-kansas-city-orche.text:
Bennie Moten, born in 1893 in Kansas City, Missouri, was an American pianist and bandleader. He led his Kansas City Orchestra, the foremost of the regional, blues-based orchestras of the Midwest in the 1920s. He helped develop the riff style that would later characterise many big bands of the 1930s, and the jazz standard Moten Swing bears his name. He died in 1935.

The orchestra made its first recordings on 23 September 1923 for OKeh. They still sounded like the New Orleans style of King Oliver and others, with the influence of ragtime and the stomping beat for which the band was known. In 1926 the band signed with Victor and let itself be influenced by the more refined style of Fletcher Henderson. In 1927 many names from Kansas City music played in it, such as Harlan Leonard, Jack Washington, Ed Lewis and Lamar Wright, with a smooth saxophone section above tinkling piano and a bass drum. In 1928 South appeared. The real change came in 1929, when Moten hired Count Basie, Walter Page and Hot Lips Page. Walter Page's walking bass lines gave the music a completely new feel, with Basie's sparing, syncopated piano figures on top. Jimmy Rushing joined as a singer. Later Ben Webster also played in the band. The last session, on 13 December 1932, gave the first traces of what would become the Basie sound, four years before Basie recorded under his own name.

In this way Moten's orchestra formed the bridge between the stomping blues of the 1920s and the swing of Count Basie. Anyone who hears the records from 1923 to 1927 hears the beginning of Kansas City jazz.
artiest/bennie-moten-s-kansas-city-orche.listen: Listen to South by Bennie Moten's Kansas City Orchestra from 1928. Notice the stomping rhythm and the way the saxophones and the brass pass short phrases to one another.

artiest/benny-andersson.text:
Benny Andersson was born in 1946 in Stockholm. His father and grandfather played the accordion, and at the age of six he was given one himself. That is how he got to know Swedish folk music and schlagers. At ten he was given a piano and taught himself to play. He listened to Elvis Presley and at fifteen left school to perform in youth clubs. In 1964 he became the keyboardist of The Hep Stars, the most popular Swedish pop band of the 1960s, for which he soon wrote hits of his own.

In 1966 he met Björn Ulvaeus, with whom he began writing songs. At the Swedish song contest of 1969 he met the singer Anni-Frid Lyngstad, and the two became a couple. Ulvaeus got together with Agnetha Fältskog. ABBA grew out of those four, and in 1974 won the Eurovision Song Contest with Waterloo. Andersson and Ulvaeus wrote and produced eight studio albums. Andersson was responsible above all for the music: rich melodies, layered arrangements and a glossy, perfectly finished studio sound.

After ABBA he continued writing with Ulvaeus. With Tim Rice they made the musical Chess (1984), with the hits I Know Him So Well and One Night in Bangkok. The Swedish musical Kristina från Duvemåla and Mamma Mia!, built on ABBA songs, followed later. He also returned to folk music, with solo albums on accordion. Andersson shows how Swedish pop music grew out of dance bands and folk music into a worldwide hit factory.
artiest/benny-andersson.listen: Listen to Dancing Queen by ABBA. Notice the piano run with which the song opens and how piano, strings and backing vocals are stacked layer upon layer into a full, sunny sound.

artiest/benny-benjamin.text:
William Benjamin, known as Benny and nicknamed Papa Zita, was born in 1925 in Birmingham, Alabama. He learned to drum in the style of the jazz big bands of the 1940s. Drummers such as Buddy Rich and Tito Puente were his models. In 1958 he became Motown's first regular studio drummer in Detroit.

As the drummer of The Funk Brothers, the label's house band, Benjamin played on a long string of hits. Early successes such as Money (That's What I Want) by Barrett Strong, Shop Around by The Miracles and Do You Love Me by The Contours carry his signature. My Girl and Get Ready by The Temptations, I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie Honey Bunch) by the Four Tops, Uptight (Everything's Alright) by Stevie Wonder and You Can't Hurry Love by The Supremes followed later. His playing was dynamic and driving. Some producers, Berry Gordy himself among them, only wanted to record when Benjamin drummed and James Jamerson played bass. The Beatles, too, were impressed.

At the end of the 1960s he became addicted to drugs and alcohol, and other drummers took over more and more of his work. He died in 1969 at the age of 43. In 2003 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Benjamin was one of the invisible forces behind the sound of Motown.
artiest/benny-benjamin.listen: Listen to You Can't Hurry Love by The Supremes. Notice Benny Benjamin's drums: a tight, thundering rhythm that, together with the bass, makes the song dance beneath Diana Ross's vocals.

artiest/benny-carter.text:
Benny Carter was an American jazz musician: saxophonist, clarinettist, trumpeter, composer, arranger and bandleader. He was born in 1907 in New York and received piano lessons from his mother and others. He played the trumpet, briefly tried the C-melody saxophone and then chose the alto saxophone. In the 1920s he played with, among others, Earl Hines and Horace Henderson's Wilberforce Collegians, of which he was bandleader until 1929. In 1927 he made his first recording, with Charlie Johnson's Paradise Ten.

As an arranger he took over Don Redman's place with Fletcher Henderson in his early twenties. He learned the trade by trying things out and by studying existing scores. His arrangements were complex, such as Keep a Song in Your Soul from 1930 for Henderson and Symphony in Riffs. He then led McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit and in 1932 a band of his own in New York with, among others, Chu Berry, Sid Catlett and Teddy Wilson. In the early 1930s he and Johnny Hodges were regarded as the best alto saxophonists in jazz, and he also became a leading trumpet soloist. In 1933 he played in the sessions with the British musician Spike Hughes. He then worked for two years as an arranger for the BBC Big Band in London and in 1938 recorded in Paris with Django Reinhardt. His albums include Cosmopolite in 1953, Jazz Giant in 1958 and Sax A La Carter! in 1960.

Carter's career continued into the twenty-first century. He helped shape the swing style with his arrangements, above all for the saxophone section, and showed how an alto saxophone with a soft, smooth tone can sing.
artiest/benny-carter.listen: Listen to Sax A La Carter! from 1960. Notice the smooth, singing tone of the alto saxophone and how every phrase sounds like a well-built arrangement.

artiest/benny-golson.text:
Benny Golson was an American tenor saxophonist, composer and arranger in bebop and hard bop, born in 1929 in Philadelphia. His mother, a seamstress and waitress, raised the family alone. He took piano lessons at the age of nine and later studied at Howard University. He then joined the rhythm and blues band of Bull Moose Jackson, in which Tadd Dameron was the pianist, whom he later regarded as his most important influence on his writing.

Between 1953 and 1959 Golson played in Dameron's band and then with Lionel Hampton, Johnny Hodges, Earl Bostic, Dizzy Gillespie and Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, with whom he recorded the classic Moanin' in 1958. In 1956, during a performance at the Apollo Theater, he heard that his friend, the trumpeter Clifford Brown, had died in a car accident. He wrote I Remember Clifford in his memory. In 1959 he founded The Jazztet with the trumpeter Art Farmer. Many of his compositions have become standards, such as Stablemates, Killer Joe, Whisper Not, Along Came Betty and Blues March. In 2021 he received the Grammy Trustees Award. He died in 2024.

Golson is regarded as one of the most important contributors to hard bop. He first came to the fore as a writer and only afterwards as a soloist. His melodies are lyrical and singable, and jazz musicians still play them today.
artiest/benny-golson.listen: Listen to I Remember Clifford. Notice the long, singing melody and the plaintive tone, which suits a song in memory of a friend who has died.

artiest/benny-goodman.text: The clarinettist Benny Goodman grew up in a poor Jewish family in Chicago. With arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, his big band broke through in August 1935 at the Palomar Ballroom in Los Angeles; he became the 'King of Swing'. On the advice of the producer John Hammond he included Black musicians in his small groups: the pianist Teddy Wilson, the vibraphonist Lionel Hampton and later the guitarist Charlie Christian. In that era of segregation it was a remarkable step. On 16 January 1938 he gave a jazz concert in Carnegie Hall that became famous. Goodman also played classical music and commissioned work from Béla Bartók, who wrote Contrasts for him.
artiest/benny-goodman.listen: Hear how the clarinet plays clear and precise above the band.

artiest/benny-goodman-and-his-orchestra.text:
Benny Goodman and His Orchestra was the big band of the clarinettist Benny Goodman, who earned the nickname King of Swing. Goodman was born in 1909 in Chicago, the son of poor Jewish immigrants. At ten he was given a clarinet at free music lessons in a synagogue. He learned from the New Orleans clarinettists who played in Chicago and was already playing in bands at fourteen. Later he worked in New York as a studio musician.

In 1934 he put together an orchestra of his own. The band played arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, who had had to disband his own Black orchestra. On 21 August 1935 the orchestra went down a storm at the Palomar Ballroom in Los Angeles. The audience cheered the fast, swinging arrangements, and that evening is often seen as the beginning of the swing era. The music was dance music for young people: horn sections bouncing riffs back and forth, a driving drummer in Gene Krupa and solos from Goodman's clear clarinet. The Carnegie Hall concert in 1938 gave jazz a place in the stately concert hall.

In a time of racial segregation Goodman played in his small groups with Black musicians, such as the pianist Teddy Wilson. In 1939 the guitarist Charlie Christian joined. Goodman at first would have nothing to do with an electric guitar, but Christian convinced him on stage. In two years Christian made the electric guitar a fully fledged jazz instrument. The orchestra launched the careers of many jazz musicians.
artiest/benny-goodman-and-his-orchestra.listen: Listen to Solo Flight from 1941, with Charlie Christian as soloist. Notice how he plays his electric guitar like a saxophonist, with long lines of fast notes, while the orchestra provides short horn stabs.

artiest/benny-goodman-trio.text:
The Benny Goodman Trio was a small jazz group within the work of the American clarinettist and bandleader Benny Goodman, who lived from 1909 to 1986. In the 1930s Goodman led one of the most popular big bands of the swing era, but he also liked to play in a small line-up. In 1935 he made recordings with a trio and a quartet, which were later released as Original Benny Goodman Trio and Quartet Sessions, Vol. 1: After You've Gone.

The group consisted of Goodman on clarinet, Teddy Wilson on piano and Gene Krupa on drums. Later Lionel Hampton joined on vibraphone, turning the trio into a quartet. That a Black pianist and vibraphonist stood together with a white bandleader on stage and in the studio was remarkable at the time. The small group had a light, transparent sound, in which every musician can be heard and the solos are given room. Such recordings from 1935 and 1936 stand alongside the big band records such as Sing, Sing, Sing. In 1938 the trio took part in the famous jazz concert in Carnegie Hall, of which a recording later appeared as 1937–1938 Jazz Concert No. 2.

The trio showed that swing was not only a matter for big orchestras. The chamber-music-like interplay of clarinet, piano and drums became a model for later small jazz groups.
artiest/benny-goodman-trio.listen: Listen to After You've Gone by the Benny Goodman Trio from 1935. Notice how the clarinet, the piano and the drums take turns, and how little is needed to swing.

artiest/benny-green.text:
Benny Green is an American hard bop pianist, born in 1963 in New York. He grew up in Berkeley, California, and had classical piano lessons from the age of seven. He was interested in jazz from an early age, since his father played tenor saxophone. Faye Carroll discovered him, and while still a teenager he played in a quintet of Eddie Henderson. At Berkeley High School he played in the school's jazz group.

In April 1983 he joined the band of Betty Carter. Later he became a member of Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. Since 1991 he has led his own trio. His first albums are Prelude from 1988, In This Direction and Lineage from 1990, followed by The Place to Be in 1994, My Gentlemen Friend in 1996 and Kaleidoscope in 1997. He recorded for Blue Note, Telarc and Criss Cross, and in 2018 Then and Now appeared on Sunnyside Records. He regularly gives workshops in the United States, including at Jazz Camp West and Jazz Port Townsend, and tours the world with his trio.

Green is compared in style to Bud Powell and Oscar Peterson, whom he also names as influences. His playing is fast, full of swing and firmly rooted in the blues, and shows that the hard bop of the 1950s is still alive for a new generation.
artiest/benny-green.listen: Listen to a track from The Place to Be from 1994. Notice the fast, flowing right hand and the blues in the left hand, which recalls Oscar Peterson.

artiest/berlin.text:
Berlin is an American new wave and synth-pop band from Los Angeles. The group grew out of The Toys, a rock band from Orange County built around the bassist John Crawford, in the late 1970s. The name Berlin had nothing to do with the German city: it was meant to make the band sound European and exotic. The musicians were inspired by Kraftwerk, Devo, Sparks and Giorgio Moroder. In 1979 the singer Terri Nunn joined, through an advertisement.

After a difficult start, the single The Metro took off. With it the band paid for the EP Pleasure Victim (1982), recorded on a tiny budget. It contained Sex (I'm a ...), which some radio stations banned because of its lyrics. The label Geffen then released the record worldwide. Love Life (1984) included No More Words, the first real hit. The biggest success came in 1986: Take My Breath Away for the film Top Gun, written and produced by Giorgio Moroder. The song won an Oscar and a Golden Globe.

That success was at the same time the end. Part of the band did not consider it a song of their own, because none of them had written it. In 1987 Berlin broke up; ten years later Nunn started again under the name. The band shows how the hit factory of the 1980s worked: a producer with a plan, a film company and a voice that fitted exactly, together good for a worldwide hit.
artiest/berlin.listen: Listen to Take My Breath Away. Notice the soft, floating synthesizer sounds and the slow electronic bass line, and the calm, breathy singing of Terri Nunn above them.

artiest/berliner-philharmoniker.text:
The Berliner Philharmoniker are a German symphony orchestra in Berlin, founded in 1882. The orchestra came into being when 54 musicians broke away from the conductor Benjamin Bilse after he wanted to take them to Warsaw in a fourth-class railway carriage, and carried on under the name Frühere Bilsesche Kapelle. Under the direction of Hans von Bülow it grew into one of the most famous orchestras in the world. In 1895 Arthur Nikisch became chief conductor, in 1923 Wilhelm Furtwängler followed, who stayed until 1945 and returned in 1952 until his death in 1954. After the war Sergiu Celibidache led the orchestra for seven years.

Herbert von Karajan was chief conductor from 1955 to 1989. Under him the orchestra recorded an enormous number of records, above all for Deutsche Grammophon, experimented with new recording techniques and toured extensively. In 1982 it hired its first female musician, the violinist Madeleine Carruzzo. In 1989, after the fall of the Wall, the orchestra for the first time democratically chose Claudio Abbado, who broadened the repertoire with modern works of the twentieth century. Simon Rattle led it from 2002 to 2018, and since 2019 Kirill Petrenko has been chief conductor. In 2009 the Digital Concert Hall began and in 2014 the orchestra's own label, Berliner Philharmoniker Recordings.

The orchestra's records show a distinctive, full and precise sound. Beethoven's Eroica, Schubert's Rosamunde and Mussorgsky's Bilder einer Ausstellung, among others, have been heard in recordings by the orchestra since the 1950s. In this way the orchestra is one of the founders of the classical record as a mass medium.
artiest/berliner-philharmoniker.listen: Listen to Beethoven's Eroica in the 1952 or 1954 recording. Notice the steady, full sound of the strings and how the winds emerge from it.

artiest/bernard-edwards.text:
Bernard Edwards was born in 1952 in Greenville, North Carolina, and grew up in Brooklyn. In the early 1970s he met the guitarist Nile Rodgers. Together they played in The Big Apple Band, and with the drummer Tony Thompson they then founded Chic. Edwards played bass and wrote and produced everything together with Rodgers.

In the late 1970s Chic made hits such as Dance, Dance, Dance, Everybody Dance, Le Freak, I Want Your Love and Good Times. Edwards and Rodgers also wrote and produced for others, with the Chic musicians playing everything except the lead vocals. That is how We Are Family and He's the Greatest Dancer by Sister Sledge and Upside Down and I'm Coming Out by Diana Ross came about. In We Are Family the singer Kathy Sledge even calls out to him to play his funky bass. Later Edwards produced the supergroup The Power Station, Robert Palmer's album Riptide and work by Rod Stewart and Duran Duran.

Edwards played tight, melodic bass lines that were just as important as the melody. His bass line from Good Times became one of the most copied pieces of music ever. It was the basis of Rapper's Delight by The Sugarhill Gang from 1979, the first rap record to become a big hit, and inspired Another One Bites the Dust by Queen. In 1996 he died in Tokyo of pneumonia, just after a concert with Rodgers. His groove lives on in disco, funk and hip hop.
artiest/bernard-edwards.listen: Listen to Le Freak by Chic. Notice Bernard Edwards's bass, which bounces melodically beneath Nile Rodgers's short, rhythmic guitar playing. Together they form the groove on which the whole song floats.

artiest/bernard-haitink.text:
Bernard Haitink was a Dutch conductor and violinist, born on 4 March 1929 in Amsterdam. He studied violin and conducting at the Amsterdam Conservatoire, first played in orchestras and in 1954 and 1955 took lessons with Ferdinand Leitner. In July 1954 he conducted his first concert with the orchestra of the Nederlandse Radio Unie. In 1956 he stood in for Carlo Maria Giulini with the Concertgebouw Orchestra, and after the sudden death of Eduard van Beinum he became that orchestra's principal conductor in 1959. From 1961 he was chief conductor, at first together with Eugen Jochum, from 1963 alone.

Haitink stayed with the Concertgebouw Orchestra until 1988 and made many recordings with them for Philips, later also for Decca and EMI. A career followed that took him across Europe and America: chief conductor of the London Philharmonic Orchestra from 1967 to 1979, music director of Glyndebourne Opera from 1978 to 1988 and of the Royal Opera House in London from 1987 to 2002. Later he led the Staatskapelle Dresden and from 2006 to 2010 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. At the Proms in London he conducted ninety concerts.

His recordings concentrate on classical and romantic symphonies and orchestral works, with cycles of Beethoven and Brahms, and symphonies by Mahler. He received Grammy Awards and in 2015 a Gramophone Award for his life's work. In a world of conspicuous conductors, Haitink was known for his calm, self-effacing style, and he showed how a Dutch conductor could belong to the world's top. He gave his last concert in September 2019.
artiest/bernard-haitink.listen: Listen to a recording of Mahler's Symphony No. 2 Resurrection from 1968 and notice how the orchestra grows from very soft to very large. Try to hear how calmly and evenly the conductor lets that build-up unfold.

artiest/bernard-herrmann.text: Bernard Herrmann was born in 1911 in New York and first worked for radio, including with Orson Welles. With Welles he made his film debut in Citizen Kane (1941). Herrmann did not like long melodies. He built his music from short motifs, which he repeated and shifted. For each film he chose an unusual instrumentation: two theremins in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), only strings in Psycho (1960). With Alfred Hitchcock he worked on, among others, Vertigo (1958) and Psycho. The screeching strings of the shower scene are world-famous. His last score, for Taxi Driver (1976), with a sultry alto saxophone, he completed shortly before his death.
artiest/bernard-herrmann.listen: Notice how a short motif of two or three notes is repeated and shifted again and again, instead of growing into a melody.

artiest/bernarda-fink.text:
Bernarda Fink is an Argentine-Slovenian mezzo-soprano, born on 29 August 1955 in Buenos Aires. Her parents came from Slovenia and had emigrated from Yugoslavia. Fink studied at the Instituto Superior de Arte of the Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires and often performed there, including with the Academia Bach. In 1985 she won first prize at the Nuevas Voces Líricas competition and left for Europe, first to Prague, where she worked with Czech orchestras. Later she lived in Carinthia in Austria. Her brother Marcos Fink is also a singer.

In the decades that followed, Fink sang with almost all the major orchestras, from the Wiener Philharmoniker to the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, under conductors such as Nikolaus Harnoncourt, René Jacobs, Philippe Herreweghe and John Eliot Gardiner. She performed in opera houses and at festivals from Salzburg to Tokyo and in halls such as Carnegie Hall. Her recordings appeared mainly on Harmonia Mundi and Hyperion, with operas by Mozart and Handel, the St Matthew Passion, songs by Schumann and Dvořák and an album Canciones argentinas from 2006.

Fink is regarded as a singer of the pre-Romantic repertoire, of Baroque opera and church music, but she was also at home in German song. That she kept Argentine folk songs in her repertoire shows that she did not let go of her South American origins. She received, among other honours, a Gramophone Award for Baroque vocal work in 2001, a Grammy Award in 2002 and in 2005 an Austrian decoration for science and art.
artiest/bernarda-fink.listen: Listen to an excerpt from her album Canciones argentinas and notice how she sings folk music with a voice trained in the classical tradition. Notice whether the sound is warm and restrained or, rather, big.

artiest/bernart-de-ventadorn.text:
Bernart de Ventadorn was a troubadour from the Occitan-speaking region, a poet and composer, who lived from about 1130 to about 1200. According to an old source he was the son of a baker at the castle of Ventadour in the Corrèze in France. There he learned singing and poetry from Viscount Eble III, and he wrote his first poems for the viscount's wife, Marguerite de Turenne. When that love came to light, he had to leave. He wandered through Montluçon and Toulouse, according to his own verses followed Eleanor of Aquitaine to the English court, later worked for Raimon V of Toulouse and probably went at the end of his life to a monastery in the Dordogne.

Of his 45 known poems, 18 have survived with music. That is more than for any other twelfth-century troubadour, and so we know more about his melodies than about those of almost all his contemporaries. His work probably dates from the years between 1147 and 1180. He wrote mainly cançons, love songs in the style called trobar leu, a clear and accessible way of writing poetry. His songs are monophonic: one singing voice, sometimes with an accompaniment that we now find difficult to reconstruct.

Bernart is regarded as the most important troubadour, in words and in music. His melodies were widely sung in northern France and the first trouvères seem to have followed him. In this way he belongs to the roots of the love song in Western popular music, the song of longing that a singer addresses to one person.
artiest/bernart-de-ventadorn.listen: Find a recording of one of his cançons, for example Can vei la lauzeta mover. Notice that there is only one melodic line and listen to how freely the singer lets that line move.

artiest/bernie-miller.text:
Bernie Miller was an American pianist and composer from Washington, D.C. He lived from 1919 to 1945 and so died before the age of thirty. Little is known about his life, and that is also apparent from what his contemporaries say about him. Gerry Mulligan later said that he had never met Miller. As far as he knew, Miller was a pianist from Washington who had already died when Mulligan got to know his music.

Yet his name has stuck in jazz because of a single composition, Bernie's Tune. The number became a jazz standard in the 1950s, above all because the Gerry Mulligan Quartet played it. With its light, pianoless sound, that group drew attention to so-called West Coast Jazz, and Bernie's Tune was part of it. In 1955 the songwriters Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller wrote lyrics for it, so that the number also existed as a vocal number.

Mulligan praised Miller's melodic sense and said that he also wrote a few other pieces that musicians liked to play. One of them was Loaded, which was recorded by, among others, Chet Baker, Stan Getz, Vido Musso, Kai Winding and Peter Griesar. Miller is thus an example of a composer whose music outlived him and became known through other musicians.
artiest/bernie-miller.listen: Find a recording of Bernie's Tune by the Gerry Mulligan Quartet and listen to the melody, which is very easy to follow. Notice how the band plays it again and again and then begins to improvise freely.

artiest/bernie-worrell.text:
Bernie Worrell was born in 1944 in Long Branch, New Jersey, and grew up in Plainfield. His mother sang in church choirs. He was a child prodigy: at three he was having piano lessons, at eight he wrote a concerto and at ten he played with members of a symphony orchestra. He studied at Juilliard in New York and at the New England Conservatory in Boston. In Plainfield he met George Clinton, the leader of the doo-wop group The Parliaments.

Clinton brought him to Detroit as keyboardist, arranger and bandleader of Parliament and Funkadelic, together called P-Funk. He was there from the first Funkadelic album in 1970. He co-wrote songs such as Flash Light and played on Mothership Connection (Star Child), Chocolate City and Atomic Dog. Worrell used piano, clavinet, Hammond organ and synthesizers by Moog and ARP. The futuristic sound of P-Funk came largely from him. His bass part on a Minimoog in Flash Light changed the sound of American R&B.

In the 1980s he played with Talking Heads, including in the concert film Stop Making Sense. Later he worked with Keith Richards, Fela Kuti and Bill Laswell. Hip hop producers such as Dr. Dre sampled his synthesizer lines, which formed the basis of the West Coast G-funk. Worrell was an accompanist with the influence of a bandleader. He died in 2016.
artiest/bernie-worrell.listen: Listen to Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker) by Parliament. Notice Bernie Worrell's high, gliding synthesizer sounds between the choruses that sing through one another.

artiest/bernt-rosengren.text:
Bernt Rosengren was a Swedish jazz saxophonist, composer and arranger. He was born on 24 December 1937 in Stockholm and died there on 15 May 2023. He was already playing professionally at nineteen at Jazz Club 57 and in 1959 in the Newport Jazz Band. He also played in the group of Lars Gullin, one of the pioneers of Swedish jazz. The Polish composer Krzysztof Komeda chose him to perform his jazz music for Roman Polanski's film Knife in the Water.

In the 1960s and 1970s Rosengren made a series of well-received records, including Stockholm Dues in 1965, Improvisations in 1969 and Notes from Underground in 1974. In Europe he played in a sextet of George Russell and worked with the trumpeter Don Cherry, who was then living in Scandinavia. In this way he moved from hard bop to post-bop and more experimental work. In the 1970s he played in Sevda, the group of the trumpeter Maffy Falay, where he picked up elements of Turkish and Middle Eastern music. He also led a big band of his own. In the 1980s he often played with American musicians such as Doug Raney, Horace Parlan and again Russell and Cherry, and in 1996 he recorded an album of songs from Porgy & Bess.

Rosengren is regarded as one of the most important figures of Scandinavian jazz. He won the Swedish Gyllene Skivan prize five times, in 1965, 1968, 1969, 1974 and 2009. In 2000 and 2003 he received awards from Django d'Or. His tone was expressive and his playing lyrical.
artiest/bernt-rosengren.listen: Listen to a piece from Notes from Underground from 1974 and notice the tone of his tenor saxophone. Ask yourself whether it sounds warm and singing, or rough and abrasive.

artiest/berry-gordy.text:
Berry Gordy was born on 28 November 1929 in Detroit, the seventh of eight children. His parents had moved north from Georgia in 1922. As a boy he wanted to be a boxer, and he boxed until he was drafted for the Korean War in 1951. Back in Detroit he opened a jazz record shop, which failed, and worked in a car factory. In the meantime he wrote songs.

His first success came in 1957, when Jackie Wilson recorded Reet Petite, a song Gordy had written with his sister Gwen and Billy Davis. Lonely Teardrops and Money (That's What I Want), among others, followed. With the young Smokey Robinson he founded a record label that grew into Motown, named after Motor Town, the nickname of Detroit. In his studio on West Grand Boulevard, which came to be called Hitsville USA, hits by The Supremes, The Temptations, Marvin Gaye, The Four Tops and Stevie Wonder came into being.

Gordy worked like the car factories of Detroit: writers, producers and regular session musicians worked on the songs as if on an assembly line. He also concerned himself with the clothing, the manners and the dance steps of his artists. In this way a polished mix of soul, rhythm and blues and gospel came into being that appealed to both a Black and a white audience. For decades Motown was the highest-earning African American business. In 1988 Gordy was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/berry-gordy.listen: Listen to Money (That's What I Want), one of the first hits from Gordy's circle. Notice the simple, constantly repeated piano figure and the raw, direct singing: considerably rougher than the polished Motown hits of later.

artiest/bert-berns.text:
Bert Berns was an American songwriter and producer who worked in the 1960s. He was born on 8 November 1929 in the Bronx in New York, the son of Russian-Jewish immigrants. As a child he contracted rheumatic fever, an illness that damaged his heart and led to his early death in 1967. He loved the music of his African American and Latin American neighbours, danced in mambo clubs and travelled to Havana. In 1960 he became a songwriter at a music publisher on Broadway.

His first hit was A Little Bit of Soap by The Jarmels in 1961. In 1962 The Isley Brothers recorded Twist and Shout, which he had written with Phil Medley, and he wrote Tell Him for The Exciters and Cry to Me for Solomon Burke. In 1963 he succeeded Leiber and Stoller as a producer at Atlantic Records, where he worked with Solomon Burke, The Drifters, Wilson Pickett and Ben E. King. He then became the first American producer to go to London to work, among others with Them. He wrote Here Comes the Night and produced Baby, Please Don't Go. In 1965 he founded the label BANG Records, with Hang on Sloopy by The McCoys, I Want Candy by The Strangeloves and Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison. In 1966 Shout Records followed for R&B and soul, with Erma Franklin and her Piece of My Heart.

Berns brought the energy of American rhythm and blues and soul to British bands, who recorded his songs. The Beatles played Twist and Shout, The Rolling Stones Cry to Me. Piece of My Heart later became a big hit for Big Brother and the Holding Company with Janis Joplin.
artiest/bert-berns.listen: Listen to Twist and Shout in the version by The Isley Brothers and notice the call and response between the lead vocal and the backing vocals. Hear how the rhythm gets you moving almost without thinking.

artiest/bert-kaempfert.text:
Bert Kaempfert was born in 1923 in Hamburg. He studied at the music school of his city and played accordion, piano, clarinet and other instruments. During the Second World War he played in a navy band. He then led a big band of his own and became an arranger and producer at the label Polydor, where he made hits with Freddy Quinn.

In 1960 he became world-famous with his orchestra through Wonderland by Night. In Germany nobody wanted to release it, but in America it reached number 1. The song had a lonely trumpet, muted brass and lush strings: the sound of easy listening. Kaempfert also wrote melodies for others. Strangers in the Night became a number 1 hit for Frank Sinatra in 1966, Spanish Eyes a hit for Al Martino, Danke Schoen the signature song of Wayne Newton and L-O-V-E a success for Nat King Cole. For Elvis Presley he adapted the German folk song Muss i denn into Wooden Heart.

In 1961 he played a part in the beginnings of The Beatles. In Hamburg he had the group accompany the singer Tony Sheridan on recordings of My Bonnie. Those were the first records on which The Beatles can be heard. When a customer in Liverpool asked for My Bonnie in Brian Epstein's record shop, Epstein went looking and discovered the band. Kaempfert afterwards let The Beatles leave without any problems, so that they could sign with George Martin.
artiest/bert-kaempfert.listen: Listen to My Bonnie by Tony Sheridan and The Beatles. Notice how the song begins slowly like an old folk song and then suddenly switches into fast rock 'n' roll with powerful guitars and drums.

artiest/bert-williams.text:
Bert Williams was born in 1874 in Nassau in the Bahamas and from the age of two or three grew up in the United States. In the late 1890s he travelled with his partner George Walker through the theatre world of minstrel shows and vaudeville. Their act consisted of songs, dance and comic dialogues, in which they reversed their roles: Walker became the self-assured dandy, Williams the seemingly sluggish simpleton. They made the cakewalk popular and, as was usual at the time, performed in blackface, although they also subtly undermined the stereotype. Williams was a master of body language and facial expression.

Nobody from 1906 became his trademark. He became the best-selling Black recording artist before 1920 and the first Black artist to have a leading role on Broadway. In 1918 the New York Dramatic Mirror called him one of the great comedians of the world. He also appeared in a film from 1914. The comedian W.C. Fields, who performed with him, called him the funniest and at the same time the saddest man he knew.

In popular music history Williams is important because he shows how a Black artist in a racist age nevertheless reached a mass audience. He became a key figure in the development of the African American entertainment world and pushed many boundaries over three decades. He died in 1922.
artiest/bert-williams.listen: Listen to Nobody. Notice how he half speaks and half sings the song, and how the timing of his pauses carries the joke and the sadness of the lyrics.

artiest/bessie-smith.text: Bessie Smith grew up in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and as a young woman travelled with tent shows, where she met Ma Rainey. In 1923 she recorded Downhearted Blues for Columbia, which sold well, and she became the best-paid Black female artist of her time: the 'Empress of the Blues'. Her voice was big and full, and she sang without a microphone to the back of a theatre. Jazz musicians such as Louis Armstrong, Fletcher Henderson and James P. Johnson played on her records. Her 1925 version of St. Louis Blues, with Armstrong, is a classic. Because of the Depression her career declined; she died in 1937 after a car accident in Mississippi.
artiest/bessie-smith.listen: Hear how voice and cornet speak in turn, as in a conversation.

artiest/beth-gibbons.text:
Beth Gibbons was born in 1965 in Exeter and grew up with her sisters on a farm in the south-west of England. At twenty-two she left for Bath and then Bristol to become a singer. There in 1991 she met Geoff Barrow on a course for would-be entrepreneurs. With Barrow and the jazz guitarist Adrian Utley she formed Portishead, for which she wrote the lyrics and sang.

The debut album Dummy appeared in 1994, with Sour Times as one of the first tracks. Portishead's music was called trip hop: slow hip hop beats, crackling samples of old film music and jazz records, and above them the fragile, melancholy voice of Gibbons. Portishead (1997) followed and, after a long pause, Third (2008). Gibbons names Edith Piaf, Billie Holiday, Nina Simone and Otis Redding as models, and you can hear that in the emotion of her singing.

Alongside Portishead she made, in 2002, the album Out of Season with Paul Webb, former bassist of Talk Talk, who called himself Rustin Man. In 2014 she sang Henryk Górecki's Third Symphony in Polish with a Polish symphony orchestra. She sang on a track by Kendrick Lamar and in 2024 released her first real solo album, Lives Outgrown. Gibbons gave the electronic music of the 1990s a human, vulnerable voice.
artiest/beth-gibbons.listen: Listen to Sour Times by Portishead. Notice the slow beat with the crackle of an old record, the tense, cinematic atmosphere of the samples and the plaintive voice of Beth Gibbons floating on top.

artiest/betty-carter.text: Betty Carter grew up in Detroit, where as a teenager she stood on stage with Charlie Parker. Bebop remained her foundation. Lionel Hampton took her into his band in 1948 and gave her the nickname 'Betty Bebop'. She sang with great freedom: tempos that suddenly speed up or slow down, melodies she made almost unrecognisable. Record companies found her difficult, and so in 1969 she founded a label of her own. She took young musicians into her trio and trained them on the bandstand. Only in 1988 did she get, with Look What I Got!, a major label and a Grammy.
artiest/betty-carter.listen: Notice how she stretches and bends a familiar melody into something new.

artiest/betty-noyes.text:
Betty Noyes was an American singer and actress, born on 11 October 1912 and died on 24 December 1987 in Los Angeles. Her name never became big, but her voice has been heard by millions of people. She began in 1938 in The Debutantes, a trio in the big band of Ted Fio Rito. In 1947 she sang in the quartet The Girlfriends, which was regularly heard on NBC radio programmes, including with Bing Crosby. She then became a singer whom studios liked to call first, one of the regular voices behind Hollywood musicals.

Her best-known work is partly invisible. In the 1952 film Singin' in the Rain she sang the numbers Would You and You Are My Lucky Star in place of Debbie Reynolds. That is remarkable, because Reynolds's character is herself, in the film, a ghost singer who sings for another actress. So Noyes sang the voice of a character who lends a voice. She also sang Baby Mine in Dumbo from 1941, uncredited, and that song was nominated for an Academy Award. She can also be heard in The Wizard of Oz, White Christmas and The Sound of Music, and she sang in Seven Brides for Seven Brothers for Ruta Kilmonis. On screen she played small roles, including in an episode of I Love Lucy.

Noyes shows how film musicals worked: the faces belonged to actors, the voices sometimes to studio singers. Without them many well-known film songs would not have sounded the way they do.
artiest/betty-noyes.listen: Watch and listen to Singin' in the Rain from 1952 and notice the singing in You Are My Lucky Star. Once you know that this is not the voice of Debbie Reynolds but that of Betty Noyes, you hear the film differently.

artiest/beyonce.text:
Beyoncé Giselle Knowles-Carter was born in 1981 in Houston, Texas. In the late 1990s she became known as the lead singer of the girl group Destiny's Child, one of the best-selling girl groups ever. She then grew into one of the biggest solo stars in the world. Like Michael Jackson, Prince and Madonna in the 1980s, she is more than a singer: she involves herself in the writing, the production, the imagery and the direction.

Her first solo album Dangerously in Love (2003) produced, with Crazy in Love, her first number 1 hit as a solo artist in the Billboard Hot 100. The double album I Am... Sasha Fierce (2008) included Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) and Halo, a piano ballad she made with Ryan Tedder. In 2013 she released the album Beyoncé without announcement, as a 'visual album' with a video for every song. Lemonade (2016) appeared together with a film of about an hour. The music ranges from blues and country to rock and hip hop, and the lyrics deal with infidelity, Black women and the history of the South. She sang the single Formation live a day after its release in the Super Bowl halftime show.

With Renaissance (2022) she looked at the history of dance music, with Cowboy Carter (2024) at that of country. For that last album she received the Grammy for Album of the Year in February 2025. With 35 Grammys she has won more than anyone else.
artiest/beyonce.listen: Halo begins quiet and low, with piano and voice. Listen to how the song grows layer by layer: heavy drums, handclaps and strings join in, until the last chorus sounds like a gospel choir at full strength.

artiest/bhupinder-singh.text:
Bhupinder Singh was an Indian ghazal singer and playback singer for Bollywood films. He was born on 6 February 1940 as Bhupinder Soin in Amritsar in Punjab and died on 18 July 2022. His father, the musician Natha Singh, was his first teacher, but a strict one: for a time Bhupinder even hated music and instruments. He began as a freelance artist at All India Radio, also worked for Doordarshan in New Delhi and learned to play the guitar. In 1962 the composer Madan Mohan heard him at a dinner party and summoned him to Bombay.

There he sang in Chetan Anand's Haqeeqat the song Hoke Majboor Mujhe Usne Bulaya Hoga, together with Mohammed Rafi, Talat Mahmood and Manna Dey. Khayyam gave him a solo in Aakhri Khat. His voice was regarded as one of the most distinctive in playback singing, and he sang duets with Kishore Kumar and Mohammed Rafi. R. D. Burman had him sing songs such as Naam Gum Jayega and Beete Na Bitaai Raina. He also released records of his own: in 1968 a first LP with three songs he had written himself, in 1978 an LP of ghazals in which he introduced Spanish guitar, bass and drums into the ghazal style, and in 1980 Woh Jo Shair Tha with lyrics by Gulzar.

In the 1980s he married the Bengali singer Mitali, and halfway through that decade he stopped playback singing. Together they made ghazal and geet cassettes and gave concerts. Singh showed how a ghazal, a lyrical love form from the South Asian tradition, could sound with Western instruments without losing its feeling.
artiest/bhupinder-singh.listen: Listen to Dil Dhoondta Hai and notice his voice, which sounds warm and slightly nasal. Try to hear how the guitar supports the singing without drowning it out.

artiest/big-boi.text:
Big Boi's real name is Antwan André Patton. He was born in 1975 in Savannah, Georgia, and as a teenager moved to Atlanta, to an aunt. His grandmother sent him and his brothers and sisters to the shop to buy singles, and an uncle played him all kinds of music, such as that of Kate Bush, his favourite artist. At Tri-Cities High School, a school for the arts and performing arts, he met André Benjamin, the later André 3000.

In 1992 the two formed OutKast and signed with LaFace Records in Atlanta. The duo made six albums and scored hits such as Ms. Jackson, So Fresh, So Clean, Roses and Elevators (Me & You). In 2003 the double album Speakerboxxx/The Love Below appeared, on which each member made a half of his own. On Speakerboxxx Big Boi stayed close to the sound of earlier OutKast records: fast, agile raps over funky, Southern beats. His single The Way You Move, with the singer Sleepy Brown, knocked André 3000's Hey Ya! off the top spot in America.

After OutKast he began a solo career. Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty (2010) was praised by critics for its inventive sound. Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors (2012) and Boomiverse (2017) followed. With OutKast, Big Boi showed that Atlanta and the American South had a distinctive, strong voice in hip hop. In 2025 he was inducted with OutKast into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/big-boi.listen: Listen to The Way You Move. Notice Big Boi's fast, rhythmic raps in the verses and Sleepy Brown's sung chorus, which gives the song a soulful and danceable character.

artiest/big-brother-en-the-holding-compa.text:
Big Brother and the Holding Company is an American rock band from San Francisco, formed in 1965 in the same psychedelic scene as the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane. The bassist Peter Albin and the guitarists Sam Andrew and James Gurley first played at jam sessions run by the organiser Chet Helms. At the start of 1966 they gave their first performance, and the drummer Dave Getz soon joined. As the house band of the Avalon Ballroom they played loud, experimental instrumental rock.

Helms felt the band needed a strong singer and brought in his friend Janis Joplin from Austin, Texas. In June 1966 she stood on stage with the band for the first time. According to Andrew she still had to learn to sing with such a loud electric band, and the band had to learn to play with a female singer. Because of Joplin the songs began to take tighter forms. The 1967 debut album sounded polite and clean, very different from the wild performances. The breakthrough came at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967. The second album Cheap Thrills (1968) did capture the band's raw power, with distorted guitars, long jams and Joplin's hoarse, soaring voice. It reached number 1 in America and is regarded as a high point of the psychedelic sound of San Francisco.

Still in 1968 Joplin left for a solo career. Big Brother made two more albums with other singers and stopped in 1972. Joplin died in 1970. Later the band reunited without her and kept performing with changing female singers.
artiest/big-brother-en-the-holding-compa.listen: Listen to Piece of My Heart from Cheap Thrills from 1968. Notice how Janis Joplin goes from whispering to screaming in the chorus, and how raw the guitars sound beneath.
